questions.problem: What is the dimension of ${\text{M}}_{4}(R),$ the vector space of all $4\times 4$ matrices over $R?$
questions.worked_solution:
The standard basis of ${\text{M}}_{n}(R)$ contains a total of ${n}^{2}$ matrices, each with one nonzero entry that is equal to $1.$ 

For example, the standard basis of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ contains ${2}^{2}=4$ elements, and is given by

$$
\{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}],\,[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\}.
$$

Therefore, for ${\text{M}}_{4}(R),$ we have

$$
\text{dim}({\text{M}}_{4}(R))={4}^{2}=16.
$$

In general, 

$$
\text{dim}({\text{M}}_{n}(R))={n}^{2}.
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following vector spaces has a dimension of $12?$

I. ${R}^{12}$

II. ${\text{M}}_{3\times 4}(R),$ the vector space of all $3\times 4$ matrices over $R$

III. ${R}_{11}[t]$, the vector space of all polynomials in the variable $t$ of degree at most $11$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of the vector spaces in turn.

I. Recall that $\text{dim}({R}^{n})=n.$ Therefore, 

  $$
  \text{dim}({R}^{12})=12.\,✓
  $$

II. Recall that $\text{dim}({\text{M}}_{n\times m}(R))=n\cdot m.$ Therefore, 

  $$
  \text{dim}({\text{M}}_{3\times 4}(R))=3\cdot 4=12.\,✓
  $$

III. Recall that $\text{dim}({R}_{n}[t])=n+1.$ Therefore, 

  $$
  \text{dim}({R}_{11}[t])=11+1=12.\,✓
  $$

Hence, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

questions.problem:
Which of the following vector spaces has a dimension of $18?$

I. ${R}_{17}[t]$, the vector space of all polynomials in the variable $t$ of degree at most $17$

II. ${\text{M}}_{6\times 3}(R),$ the vector space of all $6\times 3$ matrices over $R$

III. ${R}^{17}$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of the vector spaces in turn.

I. Recall that $\text{dim}({R}_{n}[t])=n+1.$ Therefore, 

  $$
  \text{dim}({R}_{17}[t])=17+1=18.\,✓
  $$

II. Recall that $\text{dim}({\text{M}}_{n\times m}(R))=n\cdot m.$ Therefore, 

  $$
  \text{dim}({\text{M}}_{6\times 3}(R))=6\cdot 3=18.\,✓
  $$

III. Recall that $\text{dim}({R}^{n})=n.$ Therefore, 

  $$
  \text{dim}({R}^{17})=17\ne 18.\,\times 
  $$

Hence, the correct answer is "I and II only."

questions.problem:
Which of the following vector spaces are finite-dimensional?

I. ${R}^{750}$

II. ${R}^{\infty },$ the vector space of infinite real sequences

III. ${\text{M}}_{50}(R),$ the vector space of all $50\times 50$ matrices over $R$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's examine our vector spaces.

- ${R}^{\infty }$ is *not* finite-dimensional. To understand why, we first note that the following set of sequences is linearly independent:

$$
\{{e}_{1},\,{e}_{2},\,…,{e}_{n}\},\,n\in N
$$

where, for each $j\in \{1,2,…,n\},$

$$
{e}_{j}=(0,…,0,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,{1,}_{{↑}_{{j}^{\text{th}}\text{ position}}}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,0,…).
$$

Indeed, we have that 

$$
{\sum }_{i=0}^{n}{x}_{i}{e}_{i}=0
$$

if and only if ${x}_{i}=0$ for all $i=0,1,2,…,n.$ Therefore,  for any  $n\in N,$  there exists a linearly independent subset of ${R}^{\infty }$ of size $n,$ which imples that  ${R}^{\infty }$ cannot have finite dimension.

- ${R}^{750}$ and ${\text{M}}_{50}(R)$ are finite-dimensional. Indeed, 

$$
\text{dim}({R}^{750})=750,
$$

and

$$
\text{dim}({\text{M}}_{50}(R))={50}^{2}=2\,500
$$

 
are both finite numbers.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

questions.problem: What is the dimension of ${\text{M}}_{6\times 5}(R),$ the vector space of all $6\times 5$ matrices over $R?$
questions.worked_solution:
The standard basis of ${\text{M}}_{n\times m}(R)$ contains a total of $n\cdot m$ matrices, each with one nonzero entry that is equal to $1.$ 

For example, the standard basis of ${\text{M}}_{3\times 2}(R)$ contains $3\cdot 2=6$ elements, and is given by

$$
\{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}],\,[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\}.
$$

Therefore, for ${\text{M}}_{6\times 5}(R),$ we have

$$
\text{dim}({\text{M}}_{6\times 5}(R))=6\cdot 5=30.
$$

In general, 

$$
\text{dim}({\text{M}}_{n\times m}(R))=n\cdot m.
$$
